hints: Focus on what addition polymerisation does to the C=C double bond, each alkene carbon keeps its H and Cl substituents and just gains two single bonds to the chain.
List the carbon types from the three monomers, 1,1-dichloroethene gives $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CCl}_2$ carbons while cis and trans 1,2-dichloroethene both give $\text{CHCl}$ carbons.
Remember a shown $\text{-C-C-}$ pair can come from inside one monomer or from the join between two different monomers, so check for $\text{CHCl-CHCl}$ and for mixed joins.
walkthrough:
**Identify the three monomers**

The formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{Cl}_2$ gives three alkenes. One is 1,1-dichloroethene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CCl}_2$, and the other two are cis-1,2 and trans-1,2-dichloroethene, $\text{CHCl=CHCl}$.

$$\text{CH}_2=\text{CCl}_2 \quad \text{and} \quad \text{CHCl=CHCl (cis and trans)}$$

**See what carbons go into the polymer**

In addition polymerisation the pi bond opens but substituents stay. So every chain carbon is one of these three types: $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CCl}_2$ from the 1,1-isomer, or $\text{CHCl}$ from the 1,2-isomers.

**Match sequences 1, 2 and 3**

Sequence 2 is $\text{-CHCl-CHCl-}$. This is exactly the pair inside a 1,2-monomer and between two 1,2-monomers, so it is seen.

Sequence 1 is $\text{-CCl}_2\text{-CHCl-}$ and sequence 3 is $\text{-CHCl-CH}_2\text{-}$. These are not inside a single monomer, but they occur where a 1,1-monomer joins to a 1,2-monomer in the mixed chain.

**Conclude for the mixture**

Because all three isomers polymerise together, homopolymer pairs and mixed-monomer junctions both occur. Therefore sequences 1, 2 and 3 are all seen.

options.A: Correct. Sequence 2 comes from polymerising the cis and trans 1,2-isomers. Sequences 1 and 3 come from junctions between a 1,1-unit ($\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CCl}_2$) and a 1,2-unit ($\text{CHCl}$). In a co-polymer of the mixture all three pairs appear.
options.B: False. This choice includes 1 and 2 but leaves out 3. Students choose it by spotting the $\text{CCl}_2\text{-CHCl}$ junction but forgetting the other side of the same junction gives $\text{CHCl-CH}_2$, which is sequence 3.
options.C: False. This choice includes 2 and 3 but leaves out 1. Students choose it by spotting one type of 1,1 to 1,2 join but missing that the join can be read in both directions, $\text{CCl}_2$ to $\text{CHCl}$ and $\text{CHCl}$ to $\text{CH}_2$.
options.D: False. This choice claims only sequence 2 is seen. This is the trap of thinking a $\text{-C-C-}$ unit must come from within one monomer, so only $\text{-CHCl-CHCl-}$ with the correct $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{Cl}_2$ count is allowed, and forgetting pairs that straddle two different monomers.
